query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting roughly 2 atomic percent of one refractory element with aluminum in equiatomic, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of a continuous and adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature air exposure, significantly reducing oxidation (pesting) without degrading the alloy’s excellent room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy that exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths ranging from 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor compositional modification by substituting approximately 2 atomic percent of a refractory element with aluminum, maintaining an otherwise equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in static air at 800 °C for 5 hours; subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and at high temperatures (~1000 °C) using strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a slow-growing, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 scale on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure, the minor Al addition preferentially reacts with atmospheric oxygen to form a protective Al2O3 layer. This scale acts as an effective barrier to further oxygen ingress (thus preventing pesting) while the low aluminum content minimizes any adverse effects on the intrinsic mechanical properties of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-doped alloy should show a significantly reduced oxide scale thickness and lower overall weight gain due to oxidation, while maintaining comparable room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance that leads to pesting and significant oxide scale formation under high-temperature air exposure.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature oxidation conditions (exposure in static air at 800 °C for 5 hours) and mechanical performance assessed at room temperature and at high temperatures (~1000 °C with strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al substitution level for balancing oxidation protection and mechanical integrity and the long-term adherence behavior of the formed Al2O3 scale under extended exposure remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one of the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy and one with approximately 2 atomic percent Al substituted for one refractory element. Expose both sets to static air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After oxidation, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to analyze oxide scale thickness and continuity, measure weight gains due to oxidation, and conduct tensile tests at room temperature and ~1000 °C (strain rates between 10^(-4) and 10^(-2) s^(-1)).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale thickness and weight gain, or if its room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength are significantly degraded relative to the untreated alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Oxidation resistance often controls the life of high temperature alloys in structural engineering applications. Dense, continuous and adherent Al2O3 or SiO2 oxides protect alloys from oxidation at high temperatures (T > 1000 °C). These oxides are the most protective, because of their high thermodynamic stability and the low diffusivities for anions and cations. Unfortunately, Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina formers, because in these alloys the concentration of Al must be kept low owing to the adverse effect of this element on mechanical properties (ductile to brittle transition temperature-DBTT of the Nbss, toughness, high temperature strength and creep of the alloy). Furthermore, the concentration of Si in these alloys, which can be as high as 20 at.%, cannot assure the formation of silica scale. In other words, the Nb–silicide based alloys are not alumina or silica formers. Instead, their scales consist of Ti niobates, AlNbO4, CrNbO4 and oxides of Nb and Ti [,].

AbstractPowder metallurgy possesses the advantages of low energy consumption, less material consumption, uniform composition, and near-final forming. In order to improve the mechanical properties and high-temperature oxidation resistance of CoCrNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA), CoCrNiAlX (X = 0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) MEAs were prepared using mechanical alloying (MA) and spark-plasma sintering (SPS). The effect of aluminum content on the microstructure and properties of the MEAs was investigated. The results show that the CoCrNi MEA is composed of face center cubic (fcc) phase and some carbides (Cr23C6). With the increase in Al content, there exists Al2O3 precipitation. When the Al content is increased to Al0.5 and Al0.7, the body center cubic (bcc) phase begins to precipitate. The addition of aluminum significantly enhances the properties of the alloys, especially those containing fcc+bcc dual-phase solid solutions. The yield strength, compressive strength, and hardness of CoCrNiAl0.7 alloy are as high as 2083 MPa, 2498 MPa, and 646 HV, respectively. frame.understanding: The hypothesis is that a single compositional modification – a minor addition of a reactive element (for example, substituting ~2 atomic percent of one refractory element with aluminum) – would promote the in situ formation of a protective, adherent Al2O3 scale during high-temperature exposure. This scale is expected to suppress oxygen ingress (and thus pesting) without degrading the alloy's mechanical performance. The intervention is inspired by earlier success in oxidation protection where controlled reactive-element additions in similar alloys resulted in passivating oxide scales. The hypothesis predicts that the modified equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy would demonstrate dramatically improved oxygen resistance (e.g., minimal weight gain or oxide-layer formation after 5 h exposure in air at 800 °C) compared to the untreated material, while retaining comparable tensile ductility and yield strength at room and high temperatures. A controlled experiment to falsify the hypothesis would involve fabricating two alloy variants (untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and the Al-doped version), subjecting both to identical oxidation conditions (exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 h under static load or no load), and then measuring the oxide scale thickness, weight gain, and mechanical properties. If the aluminum-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation or if its mechanical performance is degraded relative to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Over the past decade, work in refractory high‐entropy alloys has moved from establishing baseline mechanical properties in as‐cast equiatomic and near‐equiatomic systems to making subtle compositional modifications that tailor specific high‐temperature behaviors. Early studies, for instance in a related non‐equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy, demonstrated that a single reactive-element addition could inhibit pesting (i.e. low-temperature oxidation degradation) when the alloy was exposed to air at around 800 °C for 5 h. Later research in other HEAs and even in related compositions (such as the Al‐doped Ti–V–Zr–Nb system in PMC8122896) showed that minor additions of lightweight, reactive elements can encourage the in situ formation of a protective oxide (in that case, an alumina scale) without compromising the bulk mechanical properties. Despite these advances, the oxidation behavior of the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy remains unresolved.
decision.unsolved: The current gap is the lack of demonstration that the same composition‐modification strategy used in related alloys is effective in equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, while maintaining its unique combination of room- and high-temperature ductility and strength. It is not yet shown whether a minor addition of a reactive element can trigger the formation of a stable, adherent, and continuous protective oxide scale (such as Al2O3) on this composition under high-temperature air exposure.
decision.lever: Add a small (~2 atomic percent) amount of aluminum to the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, substituting one of the refractory elements, to enable the in situ formation of an adherent and protective Al2O3 scale during high-temperature air exposure.
decision.why: Reactive-element additions have already proved successful for oxidation protection in related non-equiatomic alloys and other refractory HEA systems. Aluminum is known to form a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 layer that minimizes oxygen ingress and pesting. Given that prior experiments used a similar single compositional tweak to prevent pesting at 800 °C for 5 h, this lever most directly addresses the root cause of the oxygen resistance issue while aiming to preserve the mechanical performance in both room and high temperature regimes.
